messages.content: Write an engineering team's year in review post for an internal blog. Around 250 words.

output:
Here's a draft. I've left bracketed placeholders where your team's real numbers go — swap them in, because the specifics are what keep a post like this from reading as filler.

---

**What we actually did this year**

We shipped [N] releases. Two of them were bad.

That's the honest opening, and it matters more than the good parts, because the two bad ones taught us the things we're carrying into next year. The [March] rollback cost us [six hours] of degraded checkout, and the postmortem turned up something none of us wanted to admit: our staging environment hadn't matched production since [January]. We fixed that in [April]. Nothing has rolled back since.

The rest of the year was quieter work. We cut p99 latency on [the orders API] from [840 ms to 210 ms], mostly by killing an N+1 query that had been hiding behind a cache for two years. [Priya] rewrote the deploy pipeline and took builds from [22 minutes to under 5] — the single change that people mention most in retros. We deleted [~14,000 lines] of dead code. We added [three] people to the team, and the onboarding doc they each complained about is now, finally, a good onboarding doc.

What we didn't finish: the [event-sourcing migration]. It's half-done, it's been half-done since [June], and we should decide in Q1 whether to finish it or back it out. Half-done is the worst place for it to sit.

Next year I want fewer projects and more of them landing. Thanks to everyone who carried a pager this year.

---

Word count: ~250. Two notes on structure: the "two of them were bad" opener is doing real work — if you soften it, the whole post drifts toward the usual roundup tone. And the unfinished-project paragraph is worth keeping even if it's uncomfortable, since internal posts that only list wins train people to discount them.
